title: B-29s strike Tokyo from Saipan

facts.text: At 06:15 on 24 November 1944, Brig. Gen. Emmett O'Donnell Jr., commander of the 73rd Bombardment Wing, took off from Isley Field on Saipan in the B-29 "Dauntless Dotty", leading the first B-29 strike on Tokyo.
His copilot was Maj. Robert K. Morgan, who had flown the B-17 "Memphis Belle" over Europe. Dauntless Dotty was Morgan's own B-29 of the 497th Bomb Group, named for his wife, Dorothy.
110 more B-29s followed him, 111 in all, carrying 277.5 tons of bombs. It was the first raid on Tokyo since the Doolittle Raid of April 1942.
The target was the Nakajima aircraft engine plant at Musashino, on the edge of Tokyo.
The raid had been set for 17 November. Wind and weather forced one postponement after another for a week, until the 24th dawned clear.
The wing's orders warned that 400 to 500 Japanese fighters could rise to meet the bombers. In fact the home islands had only about 375, and about 125 came up.
Over Japan the bombers flew at 27,000 to 33,000 feet into winds of about 120 knots, the jet stream. Bombs blew off course, and it proved nearly impossible to aim from that height.
Seventeen B-29s turned back. Only 24 bombed the Musashino plant; 64 more dropped on docks and city areas. Strike photos showed just 16 bomb bursts in the target area.
A Japanese pilot drove his damaged fighter into the tail of one B-29, which crashed into the sea off Honshu with all aboard. A second B-29 ran out of fuel and ditched; its crew was rescued.
The results were judged disappointing. Early in 1945 Curtis LeMay replaced Gen. Haywood Hansell at XXI Bomber Command, and in March he sent the B-29s in low, at night, with incendiaries.

O'Donnell (center, light uniform, papers in hand) talks with members of his crew under the nose of the B-29 "Dauntless Dotty" as they wait for the signal to take off for Tokyo, Saipan, November 1944. US Army Air Forces photo, National Archives 342-FH-3A38987-A64263AC (naId 204972613), use Unrestricted, US government work, public domain. Original caption calls him Maj. Gen. (his later rank); on 24 Nov 1944 he was a brigadier general. Cropped from the scanned print mount, 1600 x 1926; the lab number A-64263A.C. sits in the lower right corner, crop it out in framing. The caption does not say the photo was taken on 24 Nov itself, so credit it as November 1944. declassified.fact: The first American plane over Tokyo since the Doolittle Raid was an unarmed F-13, a photo version of the B-29. On 1 November 1944 Capt. Ralph D. Steakley's crew flew it over the city at 32,000 feet in clear weather and came home after nearly fourteen hours; the squadron lab made 7,000 prints from its film.

film.shot_notes: AAF Combat Subjects reel, silent (the WMV's audio track is only hiss), converted to H.264, 8 min 36 s. 00:00 to 00:50 color bars and leader (skip). 01:00 to 02:55 vertical target aerials of the plant area (flat, avoid as opener). 03:00 dawn over an island; 03:10 navigator and pilots in the cockpit; 03:18 to 03:35 and 04:00 a B-29 with the 497th Bomb Group's A in a square on the tail alongside. 05:22 to 05:26 B-29 close past the window with the formation beyond. NOON: open at 05:50 on the formation, a B-29 tail with A in a square in the foreground and a row of B-29s beyond (05:50 to 06:06), then Mount Fuji 06:10 to 06:16 and close 06:24 to 06:38, then B-29 tail A 2 alongside over clouds 06:40 to 06:50. 07:00 to 07:08 two B-29s over mountains; 07:10 Japanese coast and city below; 07:15 to end black. The 7 p.m. video does not use this reel (No. 088 has its own film).
film.license: Public domain, U.S. government work (U.S. Army Air Forces, NARA Record Group 18, Army Air Forces Combat Subjects). NARA use status 'Undetermined', the routine flag on these reels.
film.date_note: Not film of 24 November 1944. The record is undated; it shows B-29s of the 497th Bomb Group (A in a square on the tail), the group Dauntless Dotty belonged to (869th Bomb Squadron), flying past Mount Fuji on a later mission against the Nakajima plant at Tokyo (the record title; the Musashino plant was the Nakajima target there), probably in spring 1945 (the series number comes after 18-CS-3338, whose slates read 4 March 1945). The caption must say AAF film of a later B-29 mission to the same target, 1945. The real 24 Nov film (Dauntless Dotty boarding, O'Donnell and Hansell, the takeoff) is in 111-ADC-3043, a newsreel composite that NARA has not digitized and marks copyright, Restricted Possibly.

body:
The man in the copilot's seat of the first B-29 over Tokyo had already flown the Memphis Belle over Europe.

24 November 1944. At 06:15 Brig. Gen. Emmett O'Donnell Jr. lifted off from Isley Field on Saipan in Maj. Robert K. Morgan's own B-29, Dauntless Dotty, named for Morgan's wife, Dorothy. Morgan flew beside him, and 110 more bombers followed. It was the first raid on Tokyo since Doolittle in April 1942, aimed at the Nakajima engine plant at Musashino.

The mission had waited a week on wind and weather. The orders warned of 400 to 500 fighters. About 125 came up.

The worst trouble was higher. At 27,000 to 33,000 feet the bombers met the jet stream, and aiming became almost impossible. Seventeen turned back, and strike photos found just 16 bomb bursts in the target area.

A Japanese pilot drove his damaged fighter into the tail of one B-29, which went into the sea off Honshu with everyone aboard. By March 1945 Curtis LeMay had the bombers going in low, at night, with incendiaries.
